identity.title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
principal_investigators: Tanvir I. Farouk (PI; University of South Carolina)
Michael C. Hicks (Project Scientist; NASA GRC)
identity.platform: None (ground-based numerical modelling of ISS FLEX droplet-combustion flight data)

one_line: Detailed computer models of single burning fuel droplets, checked against droplet fires on the Space Station, explain when a droplet flame drops into a dim, low-temperature 'cool flame', how long it survives, and why the gas xenon is a poor fire suppressant.
summary: This NASA ground study (grant NNX17AF97A, 2017-2022) modelled isolated fuel droplets burning in microgravity and compared the predictions with Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) data from the ISS. A transient, spherically symmetric one-dimensional code with detailed low-temperature chemistry, spectral radiation and fibre heat loss was used. For n-heptane, n-decane and n-dodecane droplets of about 4 mm in air, a hot flame radiatively extinguishes once the flame temperature falls to about 1200 K, and the droplet continues to burn as a cool flame at 720-775 K. Longer alkanes give hotter cool flames and smaller cool-flame extinction diameters (model about 0.95, 0.43 and 0.25 mm at 1 atm). For n-dodecane, the cool-flame extinction diameter falls from about 1.9 mm at 0.5 atm to zero at 3 atm, where a 'warm' flame burns the droplet out. Methanol simulations validated on FLEX-563 gave a limiting oxygen index of about 5% with xenon, against 8-21% for other diluents. The planned three-dimensional study of convective perturbations is not in the deposited files.

question.text: The record states the aim as using FLEX flight data to quantify how imposed thermal and convective perturbations (deliberate heating, drift-induced convection) control established droplet cool flames. These are ignition, oscillation, transition to hot or warm flames, and extinction. It also aimed to explain run-to-run variability and to map stability windows for small and large droplets. The deposited documents address a narrower set of questions with spherically symmetric (unperturbed) models. Why do large n-alkane droplets in microgravity drop from a hot flame to a long-lived cool flame, and what sets cool-flame extinction? How do fuel chain length, pressure and diluent (He, CO2, Xe) change this? Can a cool flame be started directly on sub-millimetre droplets (with ozone seeding) for ground tests? Is xenon a good fire suppressant in microgravity?

physics.text: A fuel droplet in microgravity burns with a spherical diffusion flame surrounding it. Fuel vapour diffuses out, oxygen diffuses in, and heat conducted back to the surface sustains evaporation. The squared diameter falls roughly linearly in time (the d^2 law), at a burning rate K of order 0.3-0.5 mm2/s. Large droplets (do > ~3 mm) build large, strongly radiating flames. As radiation (from CO2 and H2O) and diffusive losses grow relative to heat release, the hot flame cools. Near about 1200 K the hot flame goes out ('radiative extinction'), but the droplet keeps evaporating. Alkane fuels then show 'cool flame' chemistry. This is low-temperature oxidation (about 600-800 K) through alkylperoxy (RO2), hydroperoxyalkyl (QOOH) and ketohydroperoxide intermediates, with degenerate chain branching. Over the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) range, reactivity falls as temperature rises, which allows a stable, nearly invisible flame much closer to the droplet. Such cool flames were first seen in ISS FLEX experiments in 2011, because on Earth buoyant convection shortens residence times and the flame does not survive. They matter for fire safety because a droplet can keep vaporising and partly reacting after visible flame-out. This releases unburnt fuel, aldehydes, CO and hydroperoxides, and the cool flame may later re-ignite as a hot flame. Pressure, diluent thermal diffusivity (He high, Xe very low) and chain length shift the balance between heat release and loss, and so whether hot, 'warm' (NTC, about 950 K) or cool burning persists.

sources.quote: Radiative heat loss pushes the system to transition to the second stage, cool flame burn. • A dynamic balance between heat generation and heat loss maintains the long-duration cool flame burn.

apparatus.text: Numerical models, no hardware. The main tool is the Princeton/USC transient, spherically symmetric, one-dimensional isolated-droplet combustion code. It solves gas- and liquid-phase mass, species and energy conservation, with the far field at 200 droplet radii. Its sub-models are multicomponent molecular diffusion (TRANLIB), detailed chemical kinetics and a fitted statistical narrow-band correlated-k (SNB-CK) radiation model for CO, CO2 and H2O. It also includes surface regression on an adaptive grid, evaporation and product condensation/dissolution (UNIFAC activity coefficients), a one-dimensional energy model of the tether fibre, and an optional sectional soot model. Integration is node-centred finite volume, second order on a staggered grid, with variable-order (up to fifth) backward differentiation in time. Kinetic models used were: Sarathy et al. C7-C20 (583 species, 2609 reactions) for extinction studies; Sun et al. (128/565) and Mehl et al. (652/2827) for n-heptane, with an 11-species, 26-reaction ozone subset (Reuter et al.); and Li et al. methanol (21/93). A two-dimensional axisymmetric counterflow model with and without buoyancy (DME cool diffusion flames) appears only in the 2026 seminar. The PSI record describes a three-dimensional OpenFOAM model with imposed convection and heating. No such model or result appears in any deposited file. Flight data used: FLEX (ISS Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus) droplet diameter, flame diameter and radiometer histories for n-heptane, n-decane and n-dodecane, plus methanol test FLEX-563 for xenon.

procedure.text: For each case the code is started from a cold droplet in a quiescent, uniform ambient (298 K at the far field). A thermal ignition source is deposited symmetrically around the droplet, and its energy is varied parametrically. For FLEX-563 the ignition-to-combustion energy ratio was 0.01, 0.07 or 0.25, and quasi-steady burning needed more than about 0.4 J. The run continues until extinction or burn-out. Outputs are compared with FLEX histories of droplet diameter (d/d0)^2, flame diameter, flame stand-off ratio and radiant power. The comparisons use the experimental records as published, with no extra processing by the investigators, and model inputs were not tuned to fit. Extracted observables are the average burning rate per stage, hot- and cool-flame extinction diameters, peak gas temperature, FSR and radiative and diffusive losses. Kinetic sensitivity coefficients are computed for burning rate and extinction diameter. The ozone studies seed O3 into the ambient and lower O2 below the limiting oxygen index, to test direct cool-flame initiation and oscillation in sub-millimetre droplets.

psi_data.summary: PSI-117 holds 16 files (70.8 MB), all downloaded. There are 4 conference/seminar presentations (62.5 MB, text extracted), the 2018 PhD dissertation of M. F. E. Alam (USC, 227 pp.; used as the report), a metadata zip, and 10 analysed-data files. The analysed data are figure data behind five papers. A ReadMe workbook maps each file to fuel, do, pressure, composition, DOI and figure number. All are small comma-separated tables with several side-by-side column blocks separated by empty columns, rather than tidy tables. Units are in the headers (time s, diameters mm, K mm2/s, T K, radiance W, P atm). (1) PROCI_2019_Stable_Cool (243 rows) and PROCI_2019_Oscillatory_Cool_Flame (640 rows) are model time series for a 0.5 mm n-heptane droplet with 5% O3 at 21% and 10% O2. Columns: Time, Diameter, K, T_max, D_Tmax/D_drop, D_OHm/D_drop, (D/Do)^2. (2) PROCI_C12_2019_Three_Stage (570 rows) holds FLEX n-dodecane data at 2.75 atm with He. Experimental columns: (D/Do)^2, Dflame/Do and Dflame against t/do^2 (s/mm2), two radiometer traces (W), and cool-flame diameter (HWFM and peak-to-peak). Model columns follow. (3) PROCI_2023_Alkane_Extinction_Diameter_1atm gives experimental and simulated Do, Dext_HF and Dext_CF (mm) for C7, C10 and C12 in air. (4) PROCI_2023_C12_Extinction_Diameter_vs_pressure gives Dext_HF and Dext_CF (experiment, model, error bars) at 0.5-3 atm. (5) MST_2024_Kavg (19 experimental, 6 model points) holds the cool-flame average burning rate against pressure (0.5-5 atm). MST_2024_Dext holds cool and hot extinction diameters against pressure. MST_2024_Burning_history and Radiance_Flame_Diameter (683 rows each) hold n-dodecane d^2, flame diameter, radiance and T_max histories at 0.5, 1 and 5 atm, experiment and model. Experimental points are not tied to FLEX test numbers, and the data look digitised from figures. No model input decks, source code or 3-D results are deposited.

findings.claim: In 1 atm air with do of about 4 mm, n-heptane, n-decane and n-dodecane all show two-stage burning: a hot flame, radiative extinction, then quasi-steady cool-flame burning. The hot-to-cool transition happens at a nearly universal peak flame temperature of about 1200 K, and at transition the FSR and Tmax of the three fuels are almost identical.

sources.quote: Two-stage hot-cool flame burning mode transitions are demonstrated to exist for the three fuels, and the maximum flame temperature at which transition to the second stage occurred was universally found to be ~ 1200K.
During transition to second stage burn, the FSR and the Tmax for all three fuels are almost identical.

findings.claim: Longer alkanes give more robust cool flames. Predicted cool-flame peak temperature is about 775 K for n-dodecane, 737 K for n-decane and 720 K for n-heptane, and the cool-flame burning rate rises in the same order. The cool-flame extinction diameter falls with chain length. At do = 4 mm in 1 atm air the model gives 0.95 mm (C7), 0.43 mm (C10) and about 0.25 mm (C12). FLEX measurements give 1.10-1.30 mm for C7 (do 3.3-3.9 mm), 0.66-1.32 mm for C10 and 0-0.50 mm for C12 (do 4.0-4.4 mm).

sources.quote: Tmax,CF C12 ~ 775 K > Tmax,CF C10 ~ 737 K > Tmax,CF C7 ~ 720 K • de,CF C7 > de,CF C10 > de,CF C12

findings.claim: Hot-flame extinction is governed by small-species chemistry, so all three alkanes have nearly the same hot-flame extinction diameter for a given do (model: about 3.4-3.8 mm at do of about 4 mm, rising almost one-to-one with do). The cool-flame extinction diameter also varies linearly with do, but the lines do not collapse across fuels, because low-temperature chemistry depends on carbon number.

sources.quote: High temperature combustion is strongly governed by the small species kinetics – all three fuels share nearly identical values of HF extinction diameter for the same do
Universally, de,CF for each fuel varies linearly with initial droplet diameter, but unlike de,HF these relationships do not collapse to a single function.

findings.claim: For n-dodecane (do = 4 mm, 21% O2 in N2), pressure changes the burning mode. At 1 atm or below, burning is two-stage (hot then cool), at 1.25 atm hot-cool cycling repeats, and at 3 atm a stable 'warm' (NTC) flame burns the droplet to completion. The measured cool-flame extinction diameter falls from 1.89 mm at 0.5 atm (50.7 kPa) to 0.49 mm at 0.75 atm and 0.39-0.48 mm at 1 atm, and is zero at 3 atm. The model gives 1.19, 0.41, 0.25 and 0.03 mm. The hot-flame extinction diameter stays near 3.5-3.6 mm (experiment) and 3.4-3.9 mm (model).

sources.quote: • For pressure ≤ 1.0 atm, two stage combustion – hot and cool flame extinction. • At 1.25 atm, multi-cycling of hot-cool-hot-cool flame transition. • At 3.0 atm, the system transitions to a stable “Warm” flame.

findings.claim: The n-dodecane cool-flame average burning rate rises with pressure. FLEX values are 0.315-0.333 mm2/s at 0.5 atm, 0.365-0.408 at 1 atm, 0.445-0.493 at 3 atm and 0.502-0.527 mm2/s at 5 atm. The model reproduces the trend (0.374 at 0.5 atm to 0.501 mm2/s at 5 atm) but over-predicts at 0.5 atm.

At 1.25 atm, a large (do = 7 mm) n-dodecane droplet in air is predicted to undergo four successive hot-cool flame transitions. At each transition the cool-flame temperature drops markedly and the burn time lengthens, while the hot-flame behaviour is unchanged.

sources.quote: Four “Hot-Cool” flame transition. • At every transition, the cool flame temperature decreases significantly, the burn time increases. • The hot flame behavior remains unaltered.

findings.claim: Replacing N2 with helium at 3 atm (n-heptane, do = 4 mm, 21% O2) raises the burning rate. At high He fractions (about 40%) it produces a third stage: a hot flame, then a 'warm' flame at about 950 K, then a cool flame at about 770 K. Diffusive losses dominate in the third stage. Despite the temperature drop, the flame contracts, so droplet regression barely changes. This a priori prediction was qualitatively confirmed by FLEX test 1268 (n-dodecane, 2.75 atm, 21.6% O2, 50.2% N2, 28.2% He).

sources.quote: Introduction of helium increases the burning rate, at higher helium concentration a third stage quasi-steady burn is observed 1st Stage High Temperature burn 2nd Stage Moderate Temperature burn Tflame ~ 950 K 3rd Stage Low Temperature burn Tflame ~ 770 K
The diffusive losses become prominent in the third stage “Cool flame” burn.
Experimental observation with n-dodecane at higher pressure and helium exchange validates the “a priori” numerical predictions of a three stage behaviour inferred from n-heptane simulations.

findings.claim: Xenon is a poor microgravity fire suppressant. In methanol-droplet simulations validated against FLEX-563 (do = 2.771 mm, 8% O2, 63% Xe, 1 atm), xenon gives a longer burn and a higher peak gas temperature than other diluents. Its limiting oxygen index is also far lower: about 5% for Xe, against 8% for Ar and 21% for He and CO2 (do = 1.5 mm). For Xe the LOI is about 4%, 5% and 6% for do = 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm. The cause is xenon's very low thermal diffusivity. The dissertation states that NASA postponed xenon testing as a result.

findings.claim: With ozone seeding, sub-millimetre (do = 0.5 mm) n-heptane droplets in 1 atm air (21% O2, 5% O3) are predicted to establish a cool flame directly, without a hot flame and radiative extinction. Over a range of O3, a continuous cool flame persists without a hot-flame transition. At high enough O3, initiation always leads to a hot flame. Higher-flash-point n-decane needs more O3 and has longer initial transients.

findings.claim: Near the oxygen limit (do = 0.5 mm n-heptane, 10% O2, 5% O3, 1 atm), the model gives a stable cool flame for about 0.12 s at about 710 K. This is followed by oscillations whose amplitude grows until burn-out. Oscillation starts when local O2 near the flame falls below a critical value (about 13.5% in the presentation, 12% in the dissertation). It grows because unburnt fuel leaks through the flame: about 34-46% of the fuel vapour in the flame volume appears unreacted at 1.5 x FSR. O3 at 6% or more switches the system to hot-flame burning.

findings.claim: Kinetic sensitivity analysis shows that cool-flame burning rate and extinction diameter are controlled by the competition between O2 addition to QOOH and QOOH-O2 decomposition. Speeding up the reverse reaction O2QOOH -> QOOH + O2 lowers the burning rate and raises the extinction diameter, while O2QOOH -> ketohydroperoxide + OH does the opposite. A revised kinetic model was proposed on this basis.

sources.quote: In general increase in QOOHO2 → QOOH + O2 rate decreased the burning rate and increased the extinction diameter. Vice versa QOOHO2→ Ketohydroperoxide + OH (Q = CnH2n)
The de,CF is most sensitive to: •O2QnOOH → •OQn`OOH + OH •O2QnOOH → QnOOH + O2

findings.claim: In 2-D counterflow simulations of a DME cool diffusion flame at low strain (about 90 /s, 1 atm), buoyancy lifts the flame upward. Without buoyancy, both 1-D and 2-D models place the flame at the stagnation plane, but 1-D gives steeper temperature gradients (more diffusive loss) and a slightly lower peak temperature. The conventional 1-D (OPPDIF) approach is therefore questionable for low-strain cool flames in 1 g.

sources.quote: Without buoyancy, 1D and 2D models predict the flame at or near the stagnation plane due to momentum- balanced BC.
The peak flame temperature in 1D is slightly lower compared to the 2D prediction, but the peak HRR shows the opposite trend.

findings.claim: Beyond single-component fuels, the group simulated isolated droplets of three Jet-A surrogate mixtures with the same global (fully pre-vaporised) combustion behaviour but very different distillation curves (n-decane/iso-octane/toluene; n-dodecane/iso-octane/1,3,5-trimethylbenzene; n-hexadecane/iso-octane/1,3,5-trimethylbenzene), with UNIFAC liquid-phase activity coefficients. For the first mixture, predictions agree with published drop-tower data for 550 um droplets in air once near-full internal mixing and sooting are included. Preferential vaporization depends strongly and non-linearly on initial droplet diameter and pressure: at low pressure and combustor-sized drops it is close to the frozen limit, while at practical pressures batch distillation dominates and chemical-property differences matter as much as physical ones. This is a ground (drop-tower) validation, not FLEX data.

sources.quote: The predictions using Mixture-1 are found to be in good agreement with previously published drop-tower experiments for 550 µm droplet combustion in air.
By comparing predictions for the three mixtures, preferential vaporization effects exhibit strong non-linear dependences on initial droplet diameter and ambient pressure.

However, at pressures typical of those found in applications, batch distillation dominates and preferential vaporization chemical property differences are found to become as significant as physical property effects in influencing combustion behaviors.

relevance.text: Suppression: the clearest operational result is that xenon, once considered as an agent, would support flames at very low O2 (LOI about 5% vs 21% for CO2 or He) and burn hotter and longer. It should not be used as a microgravity extinguishant. This was a model result, validated on one FLEX test. It also shows that diluent thermal diffusivity, not only heat capacity, governs inerting in the absence of buoyancy. Fundamental: in microgravity a liquid-fuel fire that appears extinguished, after radiative extinction of the visible flame, can keep burning as an invisible cool flame. It consumes fuel, releases partially oxidised species, and at elevated pressure or with He can re-ignite into hot burning (multi-cycle behaviour). Detection and post-extinguishment procedures should not assume that loss of visible flame means the end of reaction. Transferability: all results are for single, isolated, quiescent, spherically symmetric droplets of pure fuels. Ventilation flows, drift and multi-droplet or spray effects, the stated aim of this grant, are not covered by the deposited material.

habitat_conditions.text: Most n-alkane comparisons are in air (21% O2) at 0.5-5 atm (50.7-506.6 kPa), with selected He, CO2 or Xe dilution. The sub-atmospheric n-dodecane cases (0.5 and 0.75 atm = 50.7 and 76.0 kPa) bracket the pressure of a lunar habitat (O2 of 30% or more at 70.3 kPa or less). However, they used only 21% O2, so they are not at the higher O2 fraction expected there. The trend that cool-flame extinction diameter grows strongly as pressure falls (1.89 mm at 0.5 atm vs about 0.4 mm at 1 atm for n-dodecane) suggests low-pressure habitats shorten cool-flame burning. The effect of the higher O2 fraction is untested. No case approaches the spacesuit atmosphere (100% O2 at 29.6 kPa). The Earth reference is 20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa.

earth_benefits.text: Better understanding and validated models of low-temperature (cool-flame) and NTC chemistry, relevant to engine knock, multi-stage autoignition, HCCI engines, efficiency and emissions. The dissertation also refined butanol transport parameters in a widely used kinetic model.

gaps: The 3-D OpenFOAM thermo-convective perturbation study described in the PSI record (approach, hypothesis, title) is not documented in any PSI-117 file: presentations, dissertation, CSVs or ReadMe. Either it is unpublished or the record text describes the proposal. No external search was made for it.
There is no final grant report. The 'Reports' file is a 2018 PhD dissertation, so results after 2018 (PROCI 2023, MST 2024) are available only as presentation slides and CSV figure data.
The ReadMe cites the MST 2024 paper (doi 10.1007/s12217-024-10115-x), which is not in the PSI record's publication list. The PROCI 2023 extinction paper is listed.
n_tests is null: the number of simulations is not stated anywhere, and experimental CSV points are not mapped to FLEX test numbers.

The 1-atm validation slide (Extinction presentation p9) lists experiment and model dext and Kavg values for three fuels, but the extracted text does not label which panel is which fuel, so those numbers were not used. The CSV values were used instead.

Data quality (ReadMe_List_of_Data.xlsx): the XN2 column holds '74' and '85' (percent) while other rows use fractions, and the XO3 column reads 'Balance' where XO3 should be 0.05 and N2 the balance. The three-stage row gives do 4.5 mm and He 0.29, while the presentation for FLEX 1268 gives 28.2% He (and 4.40 mm in the extinction talk).

Data quality (CSVs): side-by-side blocks with blank separator columns and repeated headers. Zeros in Dext columns appear to mean 'no extinction observed or burned to completion' but are not documented. The Kavg file's experimental 'Pressure' column repeats values without test identifiers.
The critical local O2 for oscillation onset differs between the ASGSR presentation (<13.5%) and the dissertation (12%).

The metadata zip is named 'PSI-117_metadata_NEWID-13_...'. The PSI record modifiedDate (09-Jun-2026) is later than the end date, and the seminar is dated March 2026, so the record text may have been revised after the work.
